div.p: The physician Capito anointed Chryses' eyes then when he could see a high tower from a mile off and a man from a furlong and a quail from ten yards and a louse even from a foot. Now from a furlong he cannot see the town and from two hundred feet cannot see that the lighthouse is alight; he scarcely sees a horse from half a foot off and as for the quail he once saw, he can't even see a large ostrich. If he manages to give him another dose, he won't ever after be able to see even an elephant standing close to him.

div.head: 118.—Callicter
div.p: Phidon did not purge me with a clyster or even feel me, but feeling feverish I remembered his name and died.

div.head: 119.—By the Same
div.p: Whether the doctor purged or strangled the old woman no one knows, but it was terribly sudden. The noise of the clyster was in our earscp. No. 86 which this parodies. and her bier was being crowned and the rest prepared the pease-puddingA funeral dish..

div.head: 120.—By the Same
div.p: SOCLES, promising to set Diodorus' crooked back straight, piled three solid stones, each four feet square, on the hunchback's spine. He was crushed and died, but he has become straighter than a ruler.

div.head: 121.—By the Same
div.p: AGELAUS by operating killed Aecestorides, for he said, "If he had lived the poor fellow would have been lame."

div.head: 122.—By the Same
div.p: ALEXIS the physician purged by a clyster five patients at one time and five others by drugs; he visited five, and again he rubbed five with ointment. And for all there was one night, one medicine, one coffin-maker, one tomb, one Hades, one lamentation.

div.head: 123.—HEDYLUS
div.p: AGIS neither purged Aristagoras, nor touched him, but no sooner had he come in than Aristagoras was gone. What aconite has such natural virtue? Ye coffin-makers, throw chaplets and garlands on Agis.

div.head: 124.—NICARCHUS
div.p:
A. STRANGER, what dost thou seek to know? B. Who are here in earth under these tombs? A. All those whom Zopyrus robbed of the sweet day-
light, Damis, Aristoteles, Demetrius, Arcesilaus, Sos-tratus, and the next ones so far as ParaetoniumOn the Egyptian coast a considerable distance west of Alexandria. The cemetery of Alexandria did not of course extend so far..¹ For with a wooden herald's staff and counterfeit sandalsAttributes of Hermes Psychopompus; but there is some point here which eludes us.,² like Hermes, he leads down his patients to Hell.

div.head: 125.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE physician Crateas and the sexton Damon made a joint conspiracy. Damon sent the wrappings he stole from the grave-clothes to his dear Crateas to use as bandages and Crateas in return sent him all his patients to bury.

div.head: 126.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: CHARINUS anointed my eye not with a spatula, but with a three-pronged fork, and he had a new sponge like those used for paintings. In pulling out the spatula he tore out my eye from the roots and the whole spatula remained inside. But if he anoints me twice, I shall not trouble him any more by suffering from sore eyes; for how can a man who no longer has eyes do so?

div.head: On Poets (127–137) 127.—POLLIANUS
div.p: THERE are among the Muses too Avengers, who make you a poet, and therefore you write much and without judgment. Now, I entreat you, write still more, for no greater madness can I beseech the gods to give you than that.

div.head: 128.—BY THE SAMEOn a bad poet who won a prize owing to the incapacity of the other competitors, and who expected congratulations.
div.p: If I am not pleased, Florus, may I become a dactyl or a foot, one of those that you torture. Yes, I swear by the happy lot you drew in the contest, I am as pleased at your crown as if it were a joint of pork. Therefore be of good heart, Florus, and become cheerful again; in this fashion you can win the long race as well.

div.head: 129.—CEREALIUS
div.p: A poet coming to the Isthmian games to the contest, when he found other poets there said he had paristhmia (mumps). He is going to start off for the Pythian games, and if he finds poets there again he can't say he has parapythia"Parapythia" of course has no meaning. as well.

div.head: 130.—POLLIANUS
div.p: I hate these cyclicContemporary writers of epic poems. poets who say "natheless eftsoon," filchers of the verses of others, and so I pay more attention to elegies, for there is nothing I want to steal from Callimachus or Parthenius. Let me become like an "eared beast"So Callimachus calls a donkey. if ever I write "from the rivers yellow king-cupsallow celandine."Probably from Parthenius. He like Callimachus, wrote elegies. The flower is usually the so-called "greater celandine." But these epic poets strip Homer so shamelessly that they already write "Sing, O Goddess, the wrath."i.e. the very first words of his poem.

div.head: 131.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Nor water in Deucalion's day when all became water, nor Phaethon who burned up the inhabitants of the earth, slew so many men as Potamon the poet and Hermogenes by his surgery killed. So from the beginning of the ages there have been these four curses, Deucalion, Phaethon, Hermogenes and Potamon.

div.head: 132.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I HATE, Lord Caesar, those who are never pleased with any young writer, even if he says "Sing, O Goddess, the wrath," but if a man is not as old as Priam, if he is not half bald and not so very much bent, they say he can't write a b c. But, Zeus most high, if this really be so, wisdom visits but the ruptured.

div.head: 133.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Eutychides the lyric poet is dead. Fly, ye people who dwell under earth; Eutychides is coming with odes, and he ordered them to burn with him twelve lyres and twenty-five cases of music. Now indeed Charon has got hold of you. Where can one depart to in future, since Eutychides is established in Hades too?

div.head: 134.—BY THE SAME
div.p: SHALL we begin, Heliodorus? Shall we play thus at these poems together? Do you wish it, Heliodorus? "Come near, that swifter thou mayst reach Death's goal";From Iliad vi. 143. for you will see in me a master of tedious twaddle more Heliodorian than yourself.

div.head: 135.—By the Same
div.p: No longer, Marcus, no longer lament the boy, but me, who am much more dead than that child of yours. Make elegies, hangman, now for me, make dirges for me who am slain by this versy death. For all for the sake of that dead child of yours I suffer what I would the inventors of books and pens might suffer.This and the following two are skits on versifiers who insisted on reciting to their friends.

div.head: 136.—By the Same
div.p: No sword so maleficent was ever forged by man for sudden treacherous attack as is the undeclared war of murderous hexameters, Callistratus, that you come to wage with me. Sound the retreat on the bugle at once, for even Priam by his tears gained his foes' consent (?) to an armistice.A parody of Aratus, Phaen. 131.

div.head: 137.—By the Same
div.p: You serve me a slice of raw beef, Heliodorus, and pour me out three cups of wine rawer than the beef, and then you wash me out at onceTo drown like the companions of Ulysses in punishment for eating the oxen of the Sun in the island Trinacria. with epigrams. If sinning against heaven I have eaten one of the oxen from Trinacria, I would like to gulp down the sea at once³—but if the sea is too far from here, take me up and throw me into a well.

div.head: 138.—By the Same
div.p: If I only think of the grammarian Heliodorus, my tongue at once commits solecisms and I suffer from impediment of speechcp. No. 148 below..1

div.head: 139.—By the Same
div.p: Zenonis keeps Menander the bearded grammar-teacher, and says she has entrusted her son to him; but he never stops at night making her practise casesLiterally "falls.",2 conjunctions, figures, and conjugations.

div.head: 140.—By the Same
div.p: To these praters, these verse-fighters of the supper table, these slippery dominies of Aristarchus' school who care not for making a joke or drinking, but lie there playing infantile games with Nestor and Priam, cast me not literally "to be their prey and spoil.Quoted from Odyssey iii. 271."3 To-day I don't sup on "Sing, O Goddess, the wrath."

div.head: 141.—By the SameHe is ridiculing lawyers who were fond of dragging classical allusions into their speeches. Martial vi. 19 should be compared.
div.p:
I lost a little pig and a cow and one nanny-goat, and on account of them you received your little fee,
Menecles. I never had anything in common with Othryades nor do I prosecute the three hundred from Thermopylae for theft; my suit is against Eutychides, so that here how do Xerxes and the Spartans help me? I beg you just to mention me for form's sake, or I will call out loud "One thing says Menecles, and another thing says the piggie."

div.head: 142.—By the Same
div.p: After having studied "Far be it," and sphinObsolete forms. and thrice in each period, "Gentlemen of the jury," and "Here, usher, repeat the law for me," and "These presents,This way," and "I put it to you," and "two score," and "certain alleged," and indeed "By heaven," and "'Sdeath," Crito is an orator and teaches numbers of children, and to these phrases he will add gru,οὐδὲ γρῦ, "not a word," used by Demosthenes. phathi,Obsolete forms. and min.Obsolete forms.

div.head: 143.—By the Same
div.p: Pluto will not receive the rhetor Marcus when dead, saying, "Let our one dog Cerberus be enough here; but if thou wilt come in at any cost, declaim to Ixion, MelitoSee No. 246. the lyric poet, and Tityus. For I have no evil worse than thee, until the day when Rufus the grammarian shall come here with his solecisms."

div.head: 144.—Cerealis
div.p:
To use out-of-the-way wordsmagniloquent words and four or five Attic ones is not to study with proper fervour and wisdom.
To use out-of-the-way words and four or five Attic ones is not to study with proper fervour and wisdom.

For not even if you say “quaked,” and “clangs,” and “hisses,” and “gurgled,” will you be a Homer at once. Sense should underlie literature, and its phraseology be more vulgar so that people may understand what you say.

div.head: 146.—AMMIANUS
div.p: I sent Flaccus the rhetor a present of seven solecisms and received back five times two hundred. And “Now,” he says, “I send you these by the hundred, but in future when I get to CyprusHis home, where much worse Greek was talked. I will send them by the bushel.”

div.head: 147.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Asiaticus has suddenly become an orator. Nothing incredible in that! It is only another miracle in Thebes.Where so many marvels had occurred. He was presumably a Theban.

div.head: 148.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Flaccus the rhetor made solecisms the other day without even speaking, and when he was about to yawn at once was guilty of a barbarism, and now goes on making solecisms by signs with his hand, and I, seeing him, am tongue-tied.cp. No. 138, where the same phrase is used. In both cases it means “I dare not open my mouth for fear of making a solecism.”

div.head: 149.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I see the very image of you, Medon the rhetor. Well, what is there surprising in that? You have arranged your dress effectively and you are silent. Nothing could be more like.

div.head: 150.—AMMIANUS
div.p: “The rhetor Athenagoras in consequence of a dream dedicated an Arcadian hat to Arcadian Hermes.” If he is a rhetor, too, in a dream only, we will take it so inscribed to Hermes, but if he is a real one, let “Athenagoras dedicated this” suffice.The meaning, I think, is simply that if Athenagoras is a real orator, he need not announce that he is one.

div.head: 151.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This is the image of a rhetor, but the rhetor is the image of his image. How is that? He does not speak. Nothing could be more life-like.cp. No. 145.

div.head: 152.—AMMIANUS
div.p: If you want, Paulus, to teach your son to be a rhetor like all these, don’t let him learn his letters.

div.head: On Philosophers (153–158) 153.—LUCILIUS
div.p: No one at all denies, Menestratus, that you are a cynic and bare-footed and that you are shivering. But if you shamelessly steal loaves and broken pieces on the sly, I have a stick, and they call you a dog.i.e. as you are a dog (i.e. a cynic) I will beat you.

div.head: 154.—By the Same
div.p: Everyone who is poor and illiterate does not grind corn as formerly or carry burdens for small pay, but grows a beard and picking up a stick from the cross-roads, calls himself the chief dog of virtue. This is the sage pronouncement of Hermodotus, “If anyone is penniless, let him throw off his shirtThe cynics went without tunics. and no longer starve.”

div.head: 155.—By the Same
div.p: “This solid adamant of virtue, this rebuker of everyone, this fighter with the cold, with his long beard, has been caught.” “At what?” “It is not proper to say at what, but he was caught doing things that foul-mouthed people do.”

div.head: 156.—AMMIANUS
div.p: Do you suppose that your beard creates brains and therefore you grow that fly-flapper? Take my advice and shave it off at once; for that beard is a creator of lice and not of brains.

div.head: 157.—By the Same
div.p: “Good Sir” and “Can it be?” and “Whence, sirrah, and whither?” and “Right off” and “Go to” and “Quite so” and “Hie ye” and cloaky and little lock and beardie, and “Keep your little shoulder bare”—that is what present-day philosophy flourishes on.He is ridiculing two affectations of the philosophers of his day, the use of archaic forms of speech and that of diminutives. The cynics went bare-shouldered.

div.head: 158.—ANTIPATER
div.p: The wallet laments, and the fine sturdy Heracles club of Sinopian Diogenes and the double coat, foe of the cold clouds, befouled all over with encrusted dirt, lament likewise because they are polluted by thy shoulders. Verily I take Diogenes himself to be the dog of heaven, but thou art the dog that lies in the ashes. Put off, put off the arms that are not thine. The work of lions is one thing, and that of bearded goats another

div.head: On Prophets (159–164) 159.—LUCILIUS
div.p: All the astrologers as it were with one voice prophesied to my father a ripe old age for his brother. Hermoclides alone foretold his premature death, but he foretold it when we were lamenting over his corpse in the house.

div.head: 160.—By the Same
div.p: All those who take horoscopes from observing Mars and Saturn are deserving of one cudgelling. I shall see them perhaps at no distant date really learning what a bull can do and how strong a lion isi.e. exposed to beasts in the theatre..

div.head: 161.—By the Same
div.p: Onesimus the boxer came to the prophet Olympus wishing to learn if he were going to live to old age. And he said, “Yes, if you give up the ring now, but if you go on boxing, SaturnThe most unlucky of the planets. is your horoscope.”

div.head: 162.—NICARCHUS
div.p: ONE came to ask the prophet Olympicus if he should take ship for Rhodes and how to sail there safely. And the prophet said, “First have a new ship and don’t start in winter, but in summer. If you do this you will go there and back, unless a pirate catches you at sea.”

div.head: 163.—LUCILIUS
div.p: ONESIMUS the wrestler and the pentathlist Hylas and the runner Menecle sMenecles came to the prophet Olympus wishing to know which of them was going to win at the games, and he, after inspecting the sacrifice, said, “You will all win—unless anyone passes you, Sir, or unless anyone throws you, Sir, or unless anyone runs past you, Sir.”

div.head: 164.—BY THE SAME
div.p: AULUS the astrologer, after making out his own nativity, said that the fatal hour had come and that he had still four hours to live. When it reached the fifth hour and he had to go on living convicted of ignorance, he grew ashamed of PetosirisAn astrological writer. and hanged himself, and there up in the air he is dying, but he is dying ignorant.

div.head: 165.—BY THE SAME
div.p: CÆTO the miser, when he has a pain in his stomach refreshes himself by smelling not mint, but a penny piece.

div.head: 166.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ALL say you are rich, but I say you are poor, for, Apollophanes, their use is the proof of riches. If you take your share of them, they are yours, but if you keep them for your heirs, they are already someone else's.

div.head: 167.—POLLIANUS
div.p: You have money, but I will tell you how it is you have nothing. You lend all; so that in order that another may have some, you have none yourself.

div.head: 168.—ANTIPHANES.
div.p: THOU reckonest up thy money, poor wretch; but Time, just as it breeds interest, so, as it overtakes thee, gives birth to grey old age. And so having neither drunk wine, nor bound thy temples with flowers, having never known sweet ointment or a delicate little love, thou shalt die, leaving a great and wealthy testament, and of all thy riches carrying away with thee but one obol.That which it was customary to put in the corpse's mouth.

div.head: 169.—NICARCHUS
div.p: YESTERDAY, Glaucus, Dinarchus the miser being about to hang himself, did not die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence; for the rope cost sixpence, but he tried to drive a hard bargain, seeking perhaps some other cheap death. This is the very height of wretched avarice, for a man to be dying, Glaucus, and not able to die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence.

div.head: 170.—BY THE SAME
div.p: PHIDO the miser weeps not because he is dying, but because he paid thirty pounds for his coffin. Let him off this, and as there is room in it, put one of his many little children into it besides.

div.head: 171.—LUCILIUS
div.p: HERMOCRATES the miser when he was dying wrote himself his own heir in his will, and he lay there reckoning what fee he must pay the doctors if he leaves his bed and how much his illness costs him. But when he found it cost one drachma more if he were saved, " It pays," he said, " to die," and stiffened himself out. Thus he lies, having nothing but an obol, and his heirs were glad to seize on his wealth.

div.head: 172.—BY THE SAME
div.p: AULUS the miser drowned in the sea a child that was born to him, reckoning how much it would cost him if he kept it.

div.head: 173.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: If you have lent out some of it, and give some now, and are going to give some more, you are never master of your money.

div.head: On Thieves (174–184) 174.—LUCILIUS
div.p:
DIO yesterday stole CyprusCypris all of gold, just risen from her mother sea, and he also pulled down with
his hand Adonis of beaten gold and the little Love that stood by. Even the best thieves that ever were will now say, “No longer do we enter into a contest of dexterity with you.”This epigram is a parody of a subsequent one, App. Plan. 178, which should be read with it.

div.head: 175.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Eutychides stole the god himself by whom he was about to swear, saying, “I can’t swear by you.”I suppose the point is, “I can’t well swear by you that I did not steal you and thus get into trouble with you for perjury.”

div.head: 176.—BY THE SAME
div.p: As he carried off the winged Hermes, the servant of the gods, the Lord of the Arcadians, the cattle-raider, who stood here as curator of this gymnasium, Aulus the night-thief said, “Many pupils are cleverer than their teachers.”

div.head: 177.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Eutychides stole Phoebus the detector of thieves, saying, “Speak not too much, but compare thy art with mine and thy oracles with my hands and a prophet with a thief and a god with Eutychides. And because of thy unbridled tongue thou shalt be sold at once, and then say of me what thou wilt to thy purchasers.”

div.head: 178.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Herdsman, feed thy flock far away, lest Pericles the thief drive thee and thy cattle off together.

div.head: 179.—By the Same
div.p: If Dio had feet like his hands, Dio, and Hermes no longer, would be distinguished among men as winged.cp. Book XII. 75.

div.head: 180.—AMMIANUS
div.p: On the Ides (or “if you give”) Polemon does not decide the suit, on the Nones (or “if you say ‘No’The play is on the Latin non.”) he condemns you. Whether you give or don’t give, he is always Polemon.i.e. his character never changes. This Antonius Polemon the sophist, whose life by Philostratus we have, held office in Smyrna, where, as we see, he had enemies.

div.head: 181.—By the Same
div.p: We all knew, Polemon, that your name was Antonius. How is it that three letters are suddenly missing?How is it that instead of Antonius you have become “onios,” which in Greek means “venal”?

div.head: 182.—DIONYSIUS
div.p: You are killing me, a pig but not your own, and you call me “piggie” (or “our own pig”), knowing well that I am not your own.The pig was a stolen one.

div.head: 183.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Heliodorus, hearing that Saturn troubles nativities, carried off the golden Saturn at night from the temple, saying: “Experience by fact, my Lord, which of us anticipated the other in working evil, and thou shalt know which of us is the Saturn of which. ‘Who works evil for another, works it for his own heart.’A line of Callimachus. Fetch me a good price and portend what thou wilt by thy rising.”

div.head: 184.—By the Same
div.p: From the Hesperides' Garden of ZeusHe probably means "from the Emperor's garden.", Meniscus, as Heracles did formerly, carried off three golden apples. Well, what happened? When he was caught he became a famous spectacle for all, burning alive, like Heracles of old.

div.head: On Singers and Actors (185–189) 185.—By the Same
div.p: Hegelochus, my Lord Caesar, once emptied a Greek city by appearing to sing the part of NaupliusNauplius caused the destruction of the Greek fleet on its return from Troy by exhibiting deceptive beacons.. Nauplius is ever an evil to the Greeks, either sending a great wave on their ships or having a lyre-singer to play his part.

div.head: 186.—Nicarchus
div.p: The night-raven's song bodes death, but when Demophilus sings the night-raven itself dies.

div.head: 187.—Leonidas of Alexandria
div.p: Simylus the lyre-player killed all his neighbours by playing the whole night, except only Origenes, whom Nature had made deaf, and therefore gave him longer life in the place of hearing.

div.head: 188.—Ammianus
div.p: Nicetas when he sings is the Apolloi.e. perdition. The god's name is often interpreted as Destroyer. of the songs, and when he doctors, of the patients.

div.head: 189.—LUCILIUS
div.p: APOLLOPHANES the tragedian sold for five obols the stage property of five gods, the club of Heracles, Tisiphone's instruments of terror, the trident of Poseidon, the shield of Athena, and the quiver of Artemis. "And the gods that sit beside ZeusFrom Hom. Il. iv. 1." were stripped to get a few coppers to buy a little bread and wine.

div.head: On Barbers (190–191) 190.—BY THE SAME
div.p: THE barber is puzzled to know where to begin to shave the head of hairy Hermogenes, as he seems to be all head.

div.head: 191.—BY THE SAME
div.p: "ARES, Ares, destroyer of men, blood-fiend,Hom. Il. v. 455." cease, barber, from cutting me, for you have no place left in which to cut me. But change now to my muscles and my legs below the knees, and cut me there, and I will let you. For even now the shop is full of flies, and if you persist, you will see the tribes of vultures and ravens here.

div.head: On Envy (192–193) 192.—BY THE SAME
div.p: ENVIOUS Diophon, seeing another man near him crucified on a higher cross than himself, fell into a decline.

div.head: 193.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: WHAT an evil is Envy! but it has something good in it; for it wastes away the eyes and heart of the envious.

div.head: 194.—LUCILIUS
div.p: To Pan who loves the cave, and the Nymphs that haunt the hills, and to the Satyrs and to the holy Hamadryads within the cave, Marcus . . ., having killed nothing with his dogs and boar-spears, hung up the dogs themselves.

div.head: 195.—DIOSCORIDES
div.p: Aristagoras danced the part of a GallusA eunuch priest of Rhea.,¹ while I, with great labour, went through the story of the warlike Temenidae. He was dismissed with honour, but one unceasing storm of rattles sent poor Hyrnetho off the boards.The Temenidae of Euripides deal with the jealousy of their sister Hyrnetho on the part of King Temenos' sons. Into the fire with you, ye exploits of the heroes! for among the illiterate even a lark sings more musically than a swan.

div.head: On Ugly People (196–204) 196.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Bito, with a face three times worse than a monkey's, enough to make even Hecate hang herself for envy if she saw it, says, " I am chaste, Lucilius, and sleep alone ; " for perhaps she is ashamed of saying " I am a virgin." But may whoever hates me marry such a horror and have children of similar chastity.

div.head: 197.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Hieronymus formerly wanted to be too drimys (strict); now he has the dri, but the mys has turned into los.He has become drilos (i.e. striptverpus, peeled for copulation), the opposite of what he wished.

div.head: 198.—THEODORUS
div.p: “The nose’s Hermocrates”—for if we say “Hermocrates’ nose,” we give long things to little ones.Probably a proverbial phrase.

div.head: 199.—LEONIDAS OF ALEXANDRIA
div.p: Hook-nosed Sosipolis does not buy fish, but gets plenty of good fare from the sea for nothing; bringing no line and rod, but attaching a hook to his nose, he pulls out everything that swims.

div.head: 200.—By the Same
div.p: Zenogenes’ house was on fire, and he was toiling sore in his efforts to let himself down from a window. By fixing planks together he could not reach far enough, but at length, when it struck him, he set Antimachus’ nose as a ladder and escaped.

div.head: 201.—AMMONIDES
div.p: If anyone had shown Antipatra naked to the Parthians, they would have fled outside the Pillars of Heracles.

div.head: 202.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: After burying his old woman, Moschus very sensibly married a young girl, his first wife’s whole dowry remaining intact in his house. Moschus deserves to be praised for his good sense, in that he alone knows whom to poke and from whom to inherit.

div.head: 203.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: CASTOR'S nose is a hoe for him when he digs anything, a trumpet when he snores and a grape-sickle at vintage time, an anchor on board ship, a plough when he is sowing, a fishing-hook for sailors, a flesh-hook for feasters, a pair of tongs for ship-builders, and for farmers a leek-slicer, an axe for carpenters and a handle for his door. Such a serviceable implement has Castor the luck to possess, wearing a nose adaptable for any work.

div.head: 204.—PALLADAS
div.p: I WAS thunderstruck when I saw the rhetor Maurus, with a snout like an elephant, emitting a voice that murders one from lips weighing a pound each.

div.head: On Gluttons (205–209) 205.—LUCILIUS
div.p: EUTYCHIDES when he came to supper, Dionysius, did not leave AulusHis host. a single scrap, but handed everything to his servant behind him, and now Eutychides has a great supper in his house, and Aulus, not invited, sits eating dry bread.cp. Martial ii. 37.

div.head: 206.—BY THE SAME
div.p:
So may you be able, Dionysius, to digest all these things you are eating, but for custom's sake give us something to eat here too. I was invited also, and Publius served some of these things for me too to taste, and my portion too is on the board. Unless,
seeing that I am thin, you think I was ill when I sat down to table, and so watch me thus in case I eat something unnoticed by you.It looks a little as if Dionysius, the greedy guest he addresses, were a doctor.

div.head: 207.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You eat as much as five wolves, Gamus, and you hand to your slave behind you all that is over, not only your own portion, but that of those round you. But come to-morrow with your slave'sSo it appears we should understand "the man who stands at your feet." basket, and bring sawdust and a sponge and a broom.i.e. to sweep up all the fragments; he is even told to bring the sawdust which it was customary to sprinkle before sweeping.

div.head: 208.—BY THE SAME
div.p: As a racer Eutychides was slow, but he ran to supper so quickly that they said, "Eutychides is flying."

div.head: 209.—AMMIANUS
div.p: Even if thou removest thy neighbour's boundaries till thou reachest the Pillars of Heracles, a portion of earth equal to that of all men awaits thee, and thou shalt lie like Irus,The beggar in the Odyssey. with no more than an obol on thee,The obol it was customary to place in the mouth of the corpse. dissolving into the earth that is no more thine.

div.head: On Cowards (210–211)
div.p:
Aulus the soldier stops his ears when he sees charcoal or laurel, wrapping his yellow duds tight
round his headThis is the only meaning I can elicit from this possibly corrupt couplet. The soldier is supposed to be afraid of the crackling of charcoal or laurel when lighted. Yellow was a military colour.,¹ and he shudders at his own useless sword; and if you ever say, “They are coming,” he falls flat on his back. No Polemo or Stratoclides will he approach, but always has Lysimachus for a friend.He wants no friend whose name suggests war (polemos) or armies (stratos), but associates with Lysimachus (deliverer from battle).

div.head: 211.—BY THE SAME
div.p: WHEN Calpurnius the soldier saw the battle by the shipsAt Troy. painted on a wall, as is the custom, the warrior lay stretched out pulseless and pale, calling out, “QuarlerQuarter, ye Trojans dear to Ares.” Then he enquired if he had been wounded, and with difficulty believed he was alive when he had agreed to pay ransom to the wall.

div.head: On Painters (212–215)
div.p: I ordered you, Diodorus, to paint a pretty child, but you produce a child strange to me, putting a dog’s head on his shoulders, so that I weep to think how my Zopyrion was born to me by Hecuba.Said to have been changed into a dog. And finally I, Erasistratus the butcher, have got for six drachmae a son AnubisThe dog-headed god worshipped together with Isis. In Ἰσείων there is probably a pun on the Latin insicia, “sausage-meat.” from the shrines of Isis.
div.note: Said to have been changed into a dog.
The dog-headed god worshipped together with Isis. In ’Ισείων there is probably a pun on the Latin insicia, “sausage-meat.”

div.head: 213.—LEONIDAS OF ALEXANDRIA
div.p: Diodorus, painting Menodotus’ portrait, made it very like everyone except Menodotus.

div.head: 214.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Having painted Deucalion and Phaethon, Menestratus, you enquire which of them is worth anything. We will appraise them according to their own fate. Phaethon is truly worthy of the fire and Deucalion of the water.

div.head: 215.—By the Same
div.p: Eutychus the painter was the father of twenty sons, but never got a likeness even among his children.

div.head: On Lewd Livers (216–223) 216.—By the Same
div.p: You have heard of Cratippus as a lover of boys. It is a great marvel I have to tell you, but great goddesses are the Avengers. We discovered that Cratippus, the lover of boys, belongs now to another variety of those persons whose tastes lie in an inverse direction. Would I ever have expected this? I expected it, Cratippus. Shall I go mad because, while you told everyone you were a wolf, you suddenly turned out to be a kid?

div.head: 217.—By the Same
div.p: To avoid suspicion, Apollophanes married and walked as a bridegroom through the middle of the market, saying, “To-morrow at once I will have a child.” Then when to-morrow came he appeared carrying the suspicion instead of a child.

div.head: 218.—CRATES
div.p: CHOENILUSChoerilus of Samos, epic poet of the fifth century B.C. is far inferior to Antimachus, but on all occasions Euphorion would ever talk of Choerilus and made his poems full of glossesObscure words., and knew those of Philetas well, for he was indeed a follower of Homer.Such is the meaning the epigram bears on its face, but several somewhat improper puns give it the following one, reflecting not on the style but on the morals of Euphorion: But Euphorion always and everywhere had a woman's sow in his mouth, and he used to make his poems all tongue-kisses, and knew with expert accuracy the tricks of osculation; for he was indeed the real thigh-man.

div.head: 219.—ANTIPATER
div.p: I don't pay any attention, although some people are to be trusted; but in the meantime, for God's sake, if you love me, Pamphilus, don't kiss me.

div.head: 220.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Avoid the mouth of Alphaeus; he loves the bosom of Arethusa, falling headlong into the salt sea.Alluding to the story of the love of the river for the fountain Arethusa; but this epigram has also another meaning.
div.note: Alluding to the story of the love of the river for the fountain Arethusa; but this epigram has also another meaning.

div.head: 221.—AMMIANUS
div.p: I don't dislike you because you lick the sugar cane, but because you do this, too, without the cane.

div.head: 222.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ΧΕΙΛΩΝ (Chilon) and ΛΕΙΧΩΝ (licking) have the same letters. But what does that matter? For Chilon licks whether they are the same or not.

div.head: 223.—MELEAGER
div.p: You wonder whether Favorinus pokes or not; don't wonder any longer; he told me himself that he pokes with his own mouth.

div.head: 224.—ANTIPATER
div.p: When Priapus saw Cimon's prick standing upright, said he: " Oh dear! I an immortal am left behind by a mortal."

div.head: 225.—STRATO
div.p: The bed holds two submissive, and two in action—and you think they are four in all. But they're three! If you ask " How so? " count the one in the middle twice—he's jerked in a see-saw action shared by both the others.

div.head: 226.—AMMIANUS
div.p: May the dust lie light on thee when under earth, wretched Nearchus, so that the dogs may easily drag thee out.

div.head: 227.—By the Same
div.p: Sooner shall a beetle make honey or a mosquito milk than thou, being a scorpion, shalt do any good. For neither dost thou do good willingly thyself, nor dost thou allow another to do it, hated as thou art by all like Saturn's star.

div.head: 228.—By the Same
div.p: One man killed his mother, another his father, a third his brother, but Polianus all three, the first since Oedipus.

div.head: 229.—BY THE SAME
div.p: LATE in the day has the gout found him who deserved it, him who deserved to be gouty a hundred years ago.

div.head: 230.—BY THE SAME
div.p: TAKE away, Marcus, the two first letters from Mastauron, and you deserve many of what is left.i.e. many crosses (stauroi).

div.head: 231.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You are a wild beast all but a letter and a man by a letter, and you deserve many of the beasts that you are all but a letter.Addressed to Marcos. Take M away and it becomes arcos, a late form of the word arctos, "bear." He deserves many bears to tear him in pieces.

div.head: 232.—CALLIAS OF ARGOS
div.p: You were always, Polycritus, as good as gold, but now after drinking you have suddenly become a sort of rabid curse. I believe you are always wicked; wine is the test of character; it is not now that you become wicked, but now you have been shown to be so.

div.head: 233.—LUCILIUS
div.p: PHAEDRUS the man of business and the painter Rufus contended as to which of them would copy quickest and most truly. But while Rufus was about to mix his paints Phaedrus took and wrote out a renouncement of Rufus' claim faithful as a picture.i.e. admirably forged. Phaedrus owed Rufus money.

div.head: 234.—BY THE SAME
div.p: If Craterus' feet and hands were sound, his head was not, when he wrote such stuff.

div.head: 235.—DEMODOCUS
div.p: This, too, is by Demodocus: "The Chians are bad, not one bad and another not, but all bad except Procles, and Procles is a Chian.Demodocus of Leros lived previously to Aristotle who mentions him. There is another couplet identical with this except that the Lerians are substituted for the Chians and that the saying is attributed to Phocylides. Bentley's paraphrase, "The Germans in Greek are sadly to seek, Except only Hermann, and Hermann's a German," is well known."

div.head: 236.—BY THE SAME
div.p: All Cilicians are bad men, but among the Cilicians the only good man is Cinyras, and Cinyras is a Cilician.

div.head: 237.—BY THE SAME
div.p: An evil viper once bit a Cappadocian, but it died itself, having tasted the venomous blood.

div.head: 238.—BY THE SAME
div.p: The Cappadocians are always bad, but when they get a beltWhen they became soldiers. they are worse, and for the sake of gain they are the worst of all, and if once or twice they get hold of a large carriageWhen they hold high office. they are as bad as bad can be for a year. I implore thee, O King, let it not be four times, lest the whole world slide to ruin, becoming cappadocianified.The epigram must refer to some Cappadocian who looked forward to a fourth term of office.

div.head: 239.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Not Homer's Chimaera breathed such foul breath, not the fire-breathing herd of bulls of which they tell, not all LemnosThe women of Lemnos, who had killed their husbands, were afflicted by Venus with an evil odour. nor the excrements of the Harpies,See Vergil, Aen. iii. 244. nor Philoctetes' putrefying foot. So that in universal estimation, Telesilla, you surpass Chimerae, rotting sores, bulls, birds, and the women of Lemnos.

div.head: 240.—By the Same
div.p: Demostratis not only breathes herself the stink of a he-goat, but makes those who smell her breathe the same.

div.head: 241.—NICARCHUS
div.p: Your mouth and your breech, Theodorus, smell the same, so that it would be a famous task for men of science to distinguish them. You ought really to write on a label which is your mouth and which your breech, but now when you speak I think you break wind.

div.head: 242.—By the Same
div.p: I can't tell whether Diodorus is yawning or has broken wind, for he has one breath above and below.

div.head: 243.—By the Same
div.p: Onesimus went to the bath to bathe on the twelfth of the month Dystrus in the year of Antiphilus, leaving at home a child at the breast, whom when he has finished bathing he will find to be the father of two other children. . . . He writes us to say he will go again next year, for the bath-men promise to take off the heat then.The joke is evidently about a bath which it took an enormous time to heat. There appears to be something missing after the second couplet.

div.head: 244.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You bought a brass boiler, Heliodorus, colder than Thracian Boreas. Don't blow the fire, don't put your-self out; it is in vain you stir up the smoke. What you bought was a brass wine-cooler for summer.

div.head: 245.—LUCILIUS
div.p: The sides of the ship, Diophantes, let in all the waves, and through the ports ocean enters; and we see swimming in your ship herds of dolphins and the bright children of Nereus. But if we wait longer someone will soon be sailing inside this our ship, for there is no more water left in the sea.

div.head: 246.—By the SameThe joke is evidently about a bath which it took an enormous time to heat. There appears to be something missing after the second couplet.
div.p: From what quarry, Dionysius, did you hew these timbers? Of what mill-stones is the ship built? For if I know anything about it, it is a kind of lead, not oak or pine, and the lower part of me is nearly taking root.Like the Phaeacian ship in the Odyssey (xiii. 162) which Poseidon changed into a rock. Perhaps I shall suddenly become a stone, and then the worst of it is Melito will write a rotten drama about me as if I were Niobe.

div.head: 247.—By the Same
div.p:
Of a truth, Dionysius, we the seasπέλαγος may be taken either as accusative or nominative. In the former case the meaning is "we sail the seas," in the latter "we, the seas, are sailing." sail, and the ship is full of every sea from all parts. The Adriatic,
the Tyrrhene Sea, the Gulf of Issa, the Aegean, are running dry. This is no ship, but a wooden fountain of ocean. To arms, Caesar! Dionysius begins already not to command a ship, but to command the seas.

div.head: 248.—BIANOR
div.p: It was not the depths that took the ship (how the depths, when she had never sailed?) nor the south wind, but she perished before encountering south wind and sea. Already completely built, even as far as the benches, they were anointing her with the fat juice of the pine; and the pitch, overboiling with the flame of the fire, showed that she, who was being built to serve the sea faithfully, was less faithful to the land.i.e. deceived the expectations of those on the land who were building her.

div.head: 249.—LUCILIUS
div.p: MENOPHANES bought a field, and from hunger hanged himself on another man's oak. When he was dead they had no earth to throw over him from above, but he was buried for payment in the ground of one of his neighbours. If Epicurus had known of Menophanes' field he would have said that everything is full of fields, not of atoms.

div.head: 250.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE artist painted the fat man well, but to Hell with him if we shall look on two guzzlers instead of one.

div.head: 251.—NICARCHUS
div.p:
A STONE-DEAF man went to law with another stone-deaf man, and the judge was much deafer than the
pair of them. One of them contended that the other owed him five months' rent, and the other said that his opponent had ground corn at nightProbably to avoid certain dues..¹ Says the judge, looking at them: "Why are you quarrelling? She is your mother; you must both maintain her."

div.head: 252.—BY THE SAME
div.p: If you kiss meThere is a play which cannot be rendered on the two meanings of philein, to love and to kiss. you hate me, and if you hate me you kiss me. But if you don't hate me, dear friend, don't kiss me!²

div.head: 253.—LUCILIUS
div.p: From what oak-trees did your father cut you, Aristo, or from what mill-stone quarry did he hew you? For indeed you are a dancer "made of a venerable tree or of stone,"Hom. Od. xix. 163. the living original of Niobe; so that I wonder and say: "You, too, must have had some quarrel with Leto, or else you would not have been naturally made of stone."

div.head: 254.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You played in the ballet everything according to the story, but by overlooking one very important action you highly displeased us. Dancing the part of Niobe you stood like a stone, and again when you were CapaneusWho fell from the scaling-ladder struck by lightning in the legendary story of the Seven against Thebes.Who fell from the scaling-ladder struck by lightning at the siege of Thebes. you suddenly fell down. But in the case of CanaceShe killed herself when her incestuous attachment to her brother, Macareus, was discovered. you were not clever, for you had a sword, but yet left the stage alive; that was not according to the story.

div.head: 255.—PALLADAS
div.p: SNUB-NOSED Memphis danced the parts of DaphneChanged into a laurel tree. and Niobe, Daphne as if he were wooden, and Niobe as if he were of stone.

div.head: 256.—LUCILIUS
div.p: THEY say you spend a long time in the bath, Heliodora, an old woman of a hundred not yet retired from the profession. But I know why you do it. You hope to grow young, like old Pelias, by being boiled.

div.head: 257.—BY THE SAME
div.p: DIOPHANTUS saw Hermogenes the doctor in his sleep and never woke up again, although he was wearing an amulet.

div.head: 258.—BY THE SAME
div.p: AULUS the boxer dedicates to the Lord of PisaThe Olympian Zeus. his skull, having collected the bones one by one And if he escapes from Nemea, Lord Zeus, he will perchance dedicate to thee also the vertebrae he still has left.

div.head: 259.—BY THE SAME
div.p: YOU have a Thessalian horse, Erasistratus, but all the magic of Thessaly cannot make him stir; truly a wooden horse which would never have got through the Scaean gates, if all the Trojans and Greeks together had dragged it. If you take my advice, put him up as a votive statue to some god and make his barley into gruel for your children.

div.head: 260.—ANONYMOUS1 cp. No. 337.
div.p: THIS Ouleuein you had long ago, but I don't recognise the "b" (bouleuein, to be a senator), for it used to be written "d" (douleuein, to be a slave).

div.head: 261.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: PATRICIUS' son is very well behaved, as he avoids all his fellows because of impure indulgence.

div.head: 262.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE young men of Alexandria bring down Selene2 Selene (Moon) was the name of a courtesan. The words may mean "bring down the half-moon by magic," but as applied to Selene they have an improper meaning. divided in two in the ethereal night.

div.head: 263.—PALLADAS
div.p: MENANDER, standing over the comedian Paulus in his sleep, said: "I never did you any harm, and you speak me ill."

div.head: 264.—LUCILIUS
div.p: HERMON the miser, having spent money in his sleep, hanged himself from vexation.

div.head: 265.—BY THE SAME
div.p: IF an army is being led against locusts, or dog-flies, or mice, or the cavalry of fleas or frogs, you too should be afraid, Gaius, of someone enrolling you as being worthy of fighting with such foes. But if an army of brave men is being despatched, amuse yourself with something else; but the Romans do not fight against cranes.3 i.e. the Romans are not like the Pygmies, who made war on cranes, so there is no chance of their requiring your services.

div.head: 266.—BY THE SAME
div.p: DEMOSTHENIS has a lying mirror, for if she saw the truth she would not want to look into it at all.

div.head: 267.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You, Mathematician, don't require a measuring rod, and it is no concern of yours, for you have a nose three cubits long which no one grudges you.

div.head: 268.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: PROCLUS cannot wipe his nose with his hand, for his arm is shorter than his nose; nor does he say "God preserve us" when he sneezes, for he can't hear his nose, it is so far away from his ears.

div.head: 269.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I "victorious Heracles the son of Zeus" am not Lucius but they compel me to be so.A lampoon on a statue of Hercules from which Commodus had removed the head and substituted his own, inscribing it "Lucius Commodus Hercules."

div.head: 270.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Statue of the Emperor Anastasius on the Euripus.A place in the Circus at Constantinople so called.
div.p: KING, destroyer of the world, they set up this iron statue of thee as being much less precious than bronze, in return for the bloodshed, the fatal poverty and famine and wrath, by which thou destroyest all things owing to thy avarice.

div.head: 271.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Nigh to ScyllaThere must have been a statue of Scylla at the place. they set up cruel Charybdis, this savage ogre Anastasius. Fear in thy heart, Scylla, lest he devour thee too, turning a brazen goddess into small change.

div.head: 272.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: They denied their manhood and did not become women, nor were they born men, as they have suffered what women do; nor are they women, since a man's nature was theirs. They are men to women and women to men.

div.head: 273.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Your mind is as lame as your foot, for truly your nature bears outside the image of what is inside.

div.head: 274.—LUCIAN
div.p: Tell me, I ask you, Hermes, how did the soul of Lollianus go down to the house of Persephone? If in silence, it was a marvel, and very likely he wanted to teach you also something. Heavens, to think of meeting that man even when one is dead!

div.head: 275.—APOLLONIUS (RHODIUS)
div.p: Callimachus. garbage; petty toy; wooden head. Cause, the. he who wrote the Causes:—Callimachus.Callimachus the outcast, the butt, the wooden head! The origin is Callimachus who wrote the Origins.Callimachus, author of Causes or Origins (fragments are edited and translated by C. A. Trypanis, in Callimachus, Aitia etc. L.C.L. No. 421) was a librarian at Alexandria c. 250 B.C.bably written by Apollonius in the margin of an alphabetical dictionary in which stood κάλλυσμα· τὸ κάθαρμα. κ... παίγνιον. καλόπους· ὁ ξύλινος πούς. This gives it more point. τὸ² and quarrelled with his pupil the epic poet Apollonius, who, I take it, hitting at Callimachus, pretends to give two items from a word-dictionary; and I translate accordingly. The last word of the epigram is perhaps Κάλλιμάχου—E. H. W.]

div.head: 276.—LUCILIUS
div.p: INDOLENT Marcus once, when cast into prison, confessed to a murder of his own accord, being too lazy to come out.

div.head: 277.—BY THE SAME
div.p: LAZY Marcus, having once run in his sleep, never went to sleep again lest he should chance to run once more.

div.head: 278.—BY THE SAME
div.p: OUTSIDE you teach the woes of Paris and Menelaus, having at home plenty of Parises for your Helen.

div.head: 279.—BY THE SAME
div.p: NONE of the grammarians can ever be moderate, as from the very beginning he has wrath, and spite, and bileAlluding to the opening of the Iliad..

div.head: 280.—PALLADAS
div.p: BETTER to be judged by Hegemon, the slayer of robbers, than to fall into the hands of the surgeon Gennadius. For he executes murderers in just hatred, but Gennadius takes a fee for sending you down to Hades.

div.head: 281.—BY THE SAME
div.p: WHEN Magnus went down to Hades, Pluto trembled and said: "He has come to set the dead, too, on their legs."

div.head: 282.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I LAMENT no longer those who have left the sweet daylight, but those who ever live in expectation of death.

div.head: 283.—PALLADAS
div.p: MANY people say many things, but yet they cannot express in words all the currents of your vices. But there is one strange and incredible thing I marvelled at in you: how, while you were stealing, you had tears ready to hand. Coming from the land of ChalcisChalcis in Euboea. Here it probably only means the Brazen land or the land of Avarice, for which the Chalcidians were famous. We need not suppose that this magistrate was a native of Chalcis. In the next epigram he is said to come also from the Lotos-eaters' land, which was placed in North Africa. he deprived our city of brass, stealing and stealing with profitable tears.

div.head: 284.—BY THE SAME
div.p: FROM the land of the Lotophagi came the great leader Lycaon, from the land of Chalcis a fellow who gets mounted behind.from the land of Chalcis contrario more fututus.In the last word there is a play on Antioch. The prefect is here, I suppose, called Lycaon as being wolfish.

div.head: 285.—BY THE SAME
div.p: WE marvelled at another strange, effeminate characteristic. He wept while stealing, pitying those he was robbing; he who, while robbing, observed ceremonial purity, and while thus affecting purity went on despoiling, a man with nothing clean about him, not even his person free of dirt.

div.head: 286.—By the Same
div.p: “Nothing is worse than a woman, even a good one”;A verse of Menander's. and nothing is worse than a slave, even a good one. But still one requires necessary evils. Do you suppose a slave bears his master affection? A good slave would be he who broke both his legs.And consequently was incapable of doing any mischief.

div.head: 287.—By the Same
div.p: He who is cursed with an ugly wife sees darkness when he lights the lamps in the evening.

div.head: 288.—By the Same
div.p: A barber and a tailor came to blows with each other, and soon the needles got the better of the razor.He seems to be ridiculing a barber whose razors were blunt.

div.head: 289.—By the Same
div.p: O swiftest ravishment of life! A money-lender, while marking down on his tablets the interest of years, died instantly in the space of a moment, still grasping his interest in his fingers.He must have been counting out the money with his left hand and marking down the amount with his right.

div.head: 290.—By the Same
div.p: One holding in his fingers a reckoning counter for the fingers went by the counter-voteThere is a play on the two senses of psephos, “vote” and “counter.” of death in double-quick time to Hades. The counter now lives bereaved of the reckoner, whose soul is rapidly driven from hence.This epigram seems to refer to the same incident as the preceding, but is very obscure. Palladas evidently uses δακτυλικὴ ψῆφος in some sense that eludes us. What, again, is the point of his saying that the counter (or vote) is alive?

div.head: 291.—BY THE SAME
div.p: WHAT good do you do to the city by writing verses, getting so much gold for your slanders, selling iambic verses as a shopman sells oil?

div.head: 292.—BY THE SAME
div.docAuthor: On a certain Philosopher who became Prefect of Constantinople in the reign of Valentinian and Valens
div.p: THOU, seated above the heavenly wheel, hast desired a silver wheel.i.e. the official carriage. Oh, infinite shame! Erst thou wast of higher station and hast straight become much lower. Ascend hither to the depths; for now thou hast descended to the heights.The last line is merely a very frigid repetition of the opinion that the philosopher (by some said to be Themistius) demeaned himself by accepting office.

div.head: 293.—BY THE SAME
div.p: OLYMPIUS promised me a horse, but brought me a tail from which hung a horse at its last gasp.

div.head: 294.—LUCILIUS
div.p: THOU hast the wealth of a rich man, but the soul of a pauper, thou who art rich for thy heirs and poor for thyself.

div.head: 295.—BY THE SAME
div.p: IF thou hast any Dionysus in thy house, take off the ivy from his head and crown him with lettuce leaves.Addressed to a man who had given him bad wine. Lettuce, I suppose, because the wine was like vinegar. cp. No. 396.

div.head: 296.—TIMON
div.p: WHO is this who like a ram stalks through the ranks of men, a slow-coach, an Asian mill-stone of words, a spiritless block?

div.head: 297.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Tippling Old WomanThese and the following verses (No. 298) seem to have been inspired by a picture.
div.p: A. How is it, mother, that thou lovest wine more than me, thy son? Give me wine to drink since once thou didst give me milk. B. My son, my milk once stilled thy thirst, but now drink water and still thy own thirst.

div.head: 298.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
SEE how the son athirst reaches out his hand to his mother, and the woman, being a thorough woman, overcome by wine, drinking from a jar, spoke thus, looking askance: "How shall I give thee to drink, my son, from a little droppie, for this jar holds but thirty pints."
"Mother, who hast rather the harsh nature of a step-mother, give me to quaff these tears of the sweetest vine."
"Mother, evil mother, pitiless at heart, if thou lovest me, thy son, give me but a little to quaff."

div.head: 299.—PALLADAS
div.p: THOU waxest wanton! What wonder? Does it distress me? No, I bear with thee. For the boldness of the wanton is their punishment.

div.head: 300.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Thou speakest much, O man, but in a little thou shalt be laid on the ground. Silence! and while thou yet livest get into practice for death.

div.head: 301.—BY THE SAME
div.p: The Sun to men is the god of light, but if he too were insolent to them in his shining, they would not desire even light.

div.head: 302.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Thou hast not insulted me, but my poverty; but if Zeus dwelt on earth in poverty, he himself also would have suffered insult.

div.head: 303.—BY THE SAME
div.p: If I am poor, what shall it harm me? Why dost thou hate me who do no wrong? This is the fault of Fortune, not a vice of character.

div.head: 304.—BY THE SAME
div.p: All are cowards and braggarts and whatever other fault there may be among men, yet he who has reason does not expose his fault to his neighbour, but in his wisdom hides it within. But thy soul's door is flung wide open, and it is evident to all when thou crouchest in terror or art too brazen.

div.head: 305.—BY THE SAME
div.p:
Child of shamelessness, most ignorant of men, nursling of folly, tell why dost thou hold thy head high, knowing nothing? Among the grammarians
thou art the Platonist, and if anyone enquire as to Plato's doctrines thou art again a grammarian. From one thing thou takest refuge in another, and thou neither knowest the Art of Grammar nor art thou a Platonist.

div.head: 306.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Though you leave Alexandria for Antioch, and after Syria land in Italy, no man in power will ever wed you. The fact is you always are fancying that some one will, and therefore skip from city to city.

div.head: 307.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Your son is called Eros and your wife Aphrodite, and so, blacksmith, it is quite fair you should have a lame leg.i.e. like Hephaestus.

div.head: 308.—LUCILIUS
div.p: Lean Cleonicus, making a hole in his foot with the needle, himself made a hole in the needle with his foot.cp. No. 102.

div.head: 309.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Thrasymachus, you lost great wealth by a plot, and, poor fellow, you have suddenly come to naught after all your economising, lending, exacting interest, drinking water, often not even eating, so as to have a little more money. But if you calculate what starvation was then and what it is now, you have no less now than you then seemed to have.

div.head: 310.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You bought hair, rouge, honey, wax, and teeth. For the same outlay you might have bought a face.

div.head: 311.—BY THE SAME
div.p: PANTAENETUS is so lazy that when he fell sick of a fever he prayed to every god never to get up again. And now he leaves his bed unwillingly, and in his heart blames the deaf ears of the unjust gods.

div.head: 312.—BY THE SAME
div.p: THOUGH there is no one dead here now, O passer-by, Marcus the poet built a tomb here, and writing an inscription of one line as follows, engraved it : “Weep for twelve year old Maximus from Ephesus.” I (says the tomb) never even saw any Maximus, but to show off the poet’s talent I bid the passer-by weep.This phrase in Greek has also the sense of “to send to the deuce.”

div.head: 313.—BY THE SAME
div.p: ONE, bidding me to a banquet, killed me with silver hunger, serving famished dishes. And in wrath I spoke amid the silver sheen of hunger : “Where is the plenty of my earthenware dishes?”

div.head: 314.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I SOUGHT whence I should say the word pinakes (dishes) was derived, and on being invited by you I found out why they are so called. For you placed before me great pinakes of great peina (hunger), famished dishes, instruments of famine.

div.head: 315.—BY THE SAME
div.p: ANTIOCHUS once set eyes on Lysimachus’ cushion, and Lysimachus never set eyes on it again.

div.head: 316.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Milo the wrestler was once the only one who came to the sacred games, and the steward of the games called him to crown him at once. But as he was approaching he slipped and fell on his back, and the people called out: “Do not crown this man, as he got a fall when he was alone!” But he, standing up in their midst, shouted back: “Are there not three fallsTo win the match one had to throw one’s adversary three times.? I fell once; now let someone give me the other two.”

div.head: 317.—PALLADAS
div.p: Someone gave me a long-suffering donkey that moves backwards as much as forwardThe metrical foot antispastus was so called because it was composed of an iambus and a trochee, which have opposite movements. their journey’s haven to those who ride on it; a donkey, the son of slowness, a labour, a delay, a dreamThese are puns that cannot be reproduced., but first instead of lastHere there is a play on the figure of speech hysteron-proteron, or inversion of words. for those who are retiring.

div.head: 318.—PHILODEMUS
div.p: Anticrates knew the constellations much better than Aratus, but could not tell his own nativity; for he said he was in doubt whether he was born in the Ram or the Twins, or in both the Fishes. But it was clearly found to be in all three, for he is a tupper and a fool, and effeminate, and fond of fish.As μαλακός certainly refers to δίδυμοι (= Gemini, or twin testicles) I think both ὀχευτής and μωρός must refer to the Ram.

div.head: 319.—AUTOMEDON
div.p:
If you bring ten sacks of charcoal you, too, will be a citizen, and if you bring a pig, also, you will be
Triptolemus himself, and to Heraclides your intro-ducer must be given either some cabbage castocks, or lentils, or snails. Have these with you and call yourself Erechtheus, Cecrops, Codrus,Ancient Athenian heroes. whoever you like; no one minds a rap about it.He is satirizing the facility with which the Athenians granted citizenship.

div.head: 320.—ARGENTARIUS
div.p: Philostratus loved Antigone. He was poorer by five cubits, poor fellow, than Irus. The cold, how-ever, taught him a sweet remedy; for tucking up his knees (with antia gonata) he slept so, stranger, with Antigone.

div.head: 321.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: Grammarians, ye children of Stygian Momus, ye book-worms feeding on thorns,On thorny passages of authors, as we should say. demon foes of books, cubs of Zenodotus,The celebrated grammarian. soldiers of CallimachusCallimachus is a difficult poet, owing to his recondite learning. from whom, though you hold him out as a shield, you do not refrain your tongue, hunters of melancholy con-junctions who take delight in minObsolete pronouns. and sphinObsolete pronouns. and in enquiring if the Cyclops had dogs, may ye wear yourselves away for all eternity, ye wretches, muttering abuse of others; then come and quench your venom in me.

div.head: 322.—ANTIPHANES
div.p:
Idly curious race of grammarians, ye who dig up by the roots the poetry of others; unhappy book-worms that walk on thorns, defilers of the great,
proud of your ErinnaShe was reckoned among the Alexandrian poets, and hence is mentioned here together with Callimachus.,¹ bitter and dry dogs set on by Callimachus, bane of poets, darkness to little beginners, away with you, bugs that secretly bite the eloquent.

div.head: 323.—PALLADAS
div.p: Corakes (crows) and colakes (flatterers) are only distinguished by Rho and Lambda. Therefore a crow and a lick-spittle flatterer are the same thing. So, my good sir, beware of this beast, knowing that flatterers are crows that pick the living tooi.e. not, like other crows, the dead..²

div.head: 324.—AUTOMEDON
div.p: A. Accept, Phoebus, the supper I bring thee. B. I will accept it if someone lets me. A. Then, Son of Leto, is there something that thou too dost fear? B. No one else but only Arrius, for he, that ministrant of an altar that smells not of fatBecause he carries all the meat away and never lets the altar smell of fat.,³ has a more powerful claw than a robber-hawk, and once he has celebrated the processionA procession accompanying a victim for sacrifice. he walks back carrying off everything. There is great virtue in Jove's ambrosia, for I should be one of youA mortal and liable to die of starvation. if a god, too, could feel hunger.

div.head: 325.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Having supped yesterday on a leg of an old goat and the yellow stalk, ten days old, of a cabbage like hemp, I am shy of mentioning the man who invited me; for he is short-tempered, and I am not a little afraid of his asking me again.

div.head: 326.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Beard and rough hair on the thighs, how quickly time changes all! Connichus, is this what you have become? Did I not say, " Be not in all things harsh and discourteous; Beauty has its own Avenging Deities "? So you have come into the pen,i.e. as I think, " You have become tame." Commentators interpret, " You have become like a goat." proud youth; we know that you wish for it now; but then, too, you might have had sense.

div.head: 327.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA (?)Surely by the Sidonian.
div.p: Lycaenis with the dry back, the disgrace of Aphrodite, with less haunches than any deer, with whom, as the saying is, a drunken goatherd would not live. G-r-r, g-r-r! such are the wives of the Sidonians.

div.head: 328.—NICARCHUS
div.p: One day, Hermogenes and I and Cleobulus took one and the same dame, Aristodice, to a love-bed which we all shared. I myself was allotted a hoary sea to stay in—for we divided the business into one part each, not all of us getting the whole thing. But Hermogenes got a dismal mouldy lodging—the last place on earth; he dipped into an obscure spot where lie the shores which the dead haunt and breeze-tossed figs rock and roll around in the blast of horrid raucous winds. But Cheobulus—imagine him to be Zeus who was fated to climb to heaven's roof holding glowing fire in his hand. However, earth remained common ground to us all. For we spread a rush-mat on it; and that's how we parcelled out the old girl.

div.head: 329.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Demonax, do not always turn down your eyes, nor indulge your tongue; the pigi.e. as I think, "You have become tame." Commentators interpret, "You have become like a goat." has a formidable thorn. And you live . . . and sleep in Phoenicia, and though not Semele's sonDionysus, who was said to have come to maturity as a baby in the thigh of Zeus., art nourished by a thigh.

div.head: 330.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I was invited yesterday, Demetrius, and came to supper to-day. Don't find fault with me; you have a long staircase. I spent an age on it, and I should not have got safe up it to-day only I came up holding on to a donkey's tail. You touch the stars: Zeus, it seems, when he ran away with Ganymede, went up with him by this route. But from here how long will it take you to reach Hades? You are not wanting in cleverness; you have hit on a trick for being immortal.

div.head: 331.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Philo had a boat called the "Saviour," but in it perhaps not even Zeus himself can be saved. Its name only was Saviour, but the passengers sailed either close to land or to Persephone.

div.head: 332.—BY THE SAME
div.p:
Icander the captain embarked us, it seems, on his twenty-oarer, not for a sail, but to bale her out. For the water in her is not little, but Poseidon seems to sail over in her to the opposite shore. It is
the first time a ship with the dropsy has been seen. But I, at least, fear lest you may see what was once a long boat turn into our long home.There is a play on eikosoros and soros (coffin).

div.head: 333.—CALLICTER
div.p: RHODO removes leprosy and scrofula by drugs, but he removes everything else even without drugs.i.e. he is a thief.

div.head: 334.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: SOMEONE, hearing that "Damagoras" and "pestilence" were numerical equivalents,Reckoning the letters as numbers, each comes to 420 weighed the character of both from the beam of the balance. But the scale, when raised, was pulled down on Damagoras' side, and he found pestilence lighter.

div.head: 335.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: O UNHAPPY Cynegirus,A famous fighter at the battle of Marathon. The correct form of the name is Cynaegirus, the second syllable being long. The grammarian had misspelt it and made it short. how among the living and in death art thou hacked by words and axes! Formerly thy hand fell fighting in the war, and now the grammarian has deprived thee of a foot.

div.head: 336.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: CARINUS,If he be the emperor of this name, nothing is known of the circumstance to which this epigram alludes. after receiving the spoils of Asia, set sail on a winter's day at the setting of the Kids. Nemesis, too, saw the cargo, but he departed in her sight and laughing at the gods of the sea.

div.head: 337.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You are a senator, Agathinus, but tell me how much you paid now for the Beta, for formerly it was Delta.See note to the similar epigram, No. 260.

div.head: 338.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Homer taught you to call the voice enope, but who taught you to have your tongue enope (i.e. in a hole)?

div.head: 339.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You wobble your head and upwaggle your backside. One's a sign of raving at the top, the other of ravishing at the bottom.

div.head: 340.—PALLADAS
div.p: I swore ten thousand times to make no more epigrams, for I had brought on my head the enmity of many fools, but when I set eyes on the face of the Paphlagonian Pantagathus I can't repress the malady.

div.head: 341.—BY THE SAME
div.p: It is best to praise, and blaming is the cause of enmity, but yet to speak ill of others is Attic honey.

div.head: 342.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You put the ruptured man's rupture in front of him, he himself not being visible. Don't present me to the rupture; I want to see the man himself.

div.head: 343.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: SILVANUS has two servants, Wine and Sleep; he no longer loves either the Muses or his friends, but the one flowing copiously into his head charms him from bed, and the other keeps him in his bedroom snoring.

div.head: 344.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On Metrodotus, one of the VenetiThe Veneti, or Blues, were one of the factions of the Circus, the others being the Greens and Whites. who had a Green Table
div.p: METRODOTUS, detesting the eternal burden of the Greens, has this table to keep him mindful of his hatred.

div.head: 345.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: METROPHANES, swan-faced, shock-headed, lovely stork, shaking your head this way and that like a crane's, you drag your long hood over the ground.There is no point appreciable by us in these derisive lines addressed to an unknown person.

div.head: 346.—AUTOMEDON
div.p: How long, Polycarpus, sitting to feast at an empty table,i.e. his bank. The allusion in l. 7, which is partly a parody of Homer, is quite obscure. shall you live undetected on the savings of others? I no longer see you much in the market-place, but you now turn up side streets and try to think where your feet shall carry you. You promise all, "Come, take yours to-morrow. Come and get it": but not even if you take your oath do you continue to keep faith. "The wind bearing thee from Cyzicus brought thee to Samothrace": this is the goal that awaits you for the rest of your life.

div.head: 347.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: Farewell ye whose eyes ever range over the universe, and ye thorn-gathering book-worms of Aristarchus' school. What serves it me to enquire what path the Sun has run, and whose son was Proteus and who Pygmalion? Let me know works whose lines are clearLit. " white.", but let dark lore waste away the devotees of SupercallimachusesCallimachus.

div.head: 348.—ANTIPHANES
div.p: O parricide, man more savage than the beasts, all things hate thee, everywhere thy fate awaits thee. If thou fliest on the land, the wolf is near; and if thou climbest high on trees, the asp on the branches is a terror. Thou makest trial of the Nile, too, but he nourishes in his eddies the crocodile, a brute most just to the impious.

div.head: 349.—PALLADAS
div.p: Tell me whence comes it that thou measurest the Universe and the limits of the Earth, thou who bearest a little body made of a little earth? CountWe should say " measure." thyself first and know thyself, and then shalt thou count this infinite Earth. And if thou canst not reckon thy body's little store of clay, how canst thou know the measures of the immeasurable?

div.head: 350.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On a Lawyer guilty of Malpractice
div.p:
Fool, how hast thou failed to notice the balance of Justice and dost not know the sentence due to
impious men! Thou trustest in thy subtle rhetoric and thy trained mind, which knows how to utter a fallacious argument. Thou mayest hope if thou wilt, but the play of thy vain fancy cannot change Themis.

div.head: 351.—PALLADAS
div.p: I LET the cell yesterday to a barley-water maker, and to-day I found a formidable pugilist in it. And when I said, “Who art thou? Whence didst thou invade my house?” he up with his hands to box with me. I went off at the double, afraid of the savage man, on seeing the brewer suddenly turned into a bruiser. But by the boxer Pollux and Castor himself, and Zeus who hearkens to suppliants, keep the boxer, my aversion, off me; for I can’t have a stand-up fight at the beginning of every month.i.e. every time I call for the rent.

div.head: 352.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p:
SOME one questioned the musician Androtion, skilled in what concerns the lyre, on a curious piece of instrumental lore. “When you set the highest string on the right in motion with the plectron, the lowest on the left quivers of its own accord with a slight twang, and is made to whisper reciprocally when its own highest string is struck; so that I marvel how nature made sympathetic to each other lifeless strings in a state of tension.” But he swore that Aristoxenus,A celebrated writer on music. with his admirable knowledge of plectra, did not know the theoretical explanation of this. “The solution,” he said, “is as follows. The strings are all made of sheep’s gut dried all together.
So they are sisters and sound together as if related, sharing each other's family voice. For they are all legitimate children, being the issue of one belly, and they inherit those reciprocal noises. Just so does the right eye, when injured, often convey its own pain to the left eye.”

div.head: 353.—PALLADAS
div.p: Hermolycus' daughter slept with a great apei.e. an ape-like man. and she gave birth to many little ape-Hermeses. If Zeus, transformed into a swan, got him from Leda Helen, Castor, and Pollux, with Hermione at least a crow lay, and, poor woman, she gave birth to a Hermes-crowd of horrible demons.The epigram seems very confused. Is Hermione the same as Hermolycus' daughter, and how did she manage to have such a variety of husbands?

div.head: 354.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p:
One enquired as follows about the soul from Nicostratus, that second Aristotle, that equal of Plato, the straw-splitter of the loftiest philosophy. “How should we describe the soul, as mortal or rather immortal? Must we call it a body or incorporeal? Is it to be classed among intelligible or apprehensible things, or is it both?” But he perused again his books of metaphysic and Aristotle's work on the Soul, and having renewed his acquaintance with Plato's sublimity in the Phaedo, armed himself from every source with the complete truth. Then, wrapping his cloak about him and stroking down the end of his beard, he gave utter-
ance to the solution : " If the soul has in truth any nature (for even that I don't know) it is in any case either mortal or immortal, either of a solid nature or immaterial ; but when you have passed over Acheron, there you shall learn the precise truth like Plato. Or, if you will, imitate the boy Cleombrotus of AmbraciaSee Callimachus epigram, Bk. VII. 471.,¹ and let your body drop from the roof. Then you would at once recognise what you are, being without a body, and with nothing left you but the thing you are enquiring into."

div.head: 355.—PALLADAS
div.p: You say " I know all things," but you are imperfect in all things. Tasting of everything, you have nothing that is your own.

div.head: 356.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: The book of Homer, which never lies, lied about thee, saying the minds of young men are volatile.

div.head: 357.—PALLADAS
div.p: A son and father started a competitive contest as to which could eat up all the property by spending most, and after devouring absolutely all the money they have at last each other to eat up.

div.head: 358.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Rufinianus was once Rufus in two syllables, but extended his syllables simultaneously with his crimes; but he does not escape the eye of two-syllabled Justice, for he shall again be called in two syllables Rufus the scoundrel and rascal, as he was before.

div.head: 359.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: O thou who art higher than all power, save my wretched self from all envy. Thou wouldest hear and I, too, would speak; for the wish gives birth to double pleasure, while elegance on the speaker's part and gravity on the hearer's bestow double beauty on the speech. Thou art the luminary of speech and of laws, judging by law and excelling in speech. I saw in this prince a cat-like goldThis obscure vituperation conveys very little to us. Were the two brothers members of the general's staff? That they are all called Hermeses implies that they were thieves.-grabber or a cruel leech, a mass of bile set in gold.1

div.head: 360.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Now the general has become Hermanubis the dog, taking with him two brother Hermeses, stealers of silver, tied together with a rope, cold, prematurely dead demons of TartarusIl. i. 502..2 I know no place that accuses morals, but I say that morals accuse the place.

div.head: 361.—AUTOMEDON
div.p: Two mules, equally advanced in years, adorn my carriage, in all things resembling Homer's PrayersWho was lame.: lame, wrinkled, with squinting eyes, the escort of Hephaestus,4 leathery demons who never tasted, I swear it by the Sun, even in a dream, either barley in summer or grass in spring. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, may you live as long as a crow or stag, feeding on empty air.

div.head: 362.—CALLIMACHUS
div.p: ORESTES of old, Leucarus, was happy in this, that, mad in other matters, he was not mad with my madness, nor did he have to apply the test to the PhocianPylades, the friend of Orestes.,¹ which is the trial of a friend, but taught him a part in one drama only. Perchance had he done this he would have lost his companion, and, as a fact, I no longer have most of my Pyladeses.The point of the whole has not been explained, and it is unfortunate that line 4 is corrupt. The "one drama" must, I think, mean the Choephori. Orestes then would have offended Pylades had he introduced him into the Eumenides also, and Callimachus had offended his friends in some like manner.

div.head: 363.—DIOSCORIDES
div.p: GONE is the honour of the Alexandrians and Moschus, Ptolemaeus'It is scarcely probable that he means the King. The name, of course, is fairly common. son, has won glory among the young men in the torch-race, Moschus, Ptolemaeus' son! Woe for my city! And where are his mother's deeds of shame and her public prostitution?Literally, "work on the roof." The calling of a prostitute is still called "work" in Greece. Where are the . . .? Where are the pigsties? Bring forth, ye whores, bring forth, persuaded by Moschus' crown.

div.head: 364.—BIANOR
div.p: THIS man, a cypher, mean, yes a slave, this man look ye, is lord of some other's soul.

div.head: 365.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p:
CALLIGENES the husbandman, when he had cast the seed into the land, came to the house of Aristophanes
the astrologer and begged him to tell him if he would have a favourable harvest and great abundance of corn. Taking his counters and spreading them on a tray, and bending his fingers, he said to Calligenes: "If your bit of land receives sufficient rain and produces no crop of wild flowers, if the frost does not break the furrows, if the hail does not nip off the tops of the sprouting ears, if no goat browses on the corn, and if it meet with no other injury by air or earth, I prophesy that your harvest will be excellent and you will cut the ears with success; only look out for the locusts."

div.head: 366.—MACEDONIUS THE CONSUL
div.p: A parsimonious man, laying hands on a treasure in a dream, wished to die enjoying a rich sleep. But when after the shadowy gain of the dream he awoke and saw his poverty as it was, he went to sleep again.

div.head: 367.—JULIAN ANTECESSOR
div.p: You have a face just like an ostrich. Did Circe give you a potion to drink and change your nature into that of a bird?

div.head: 368.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You have such a heavy crop on your hairy face that you ought to have it cut with scythes and not with scissors.

div.head: 369.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Live in safety in the town, lest the stork who delights in the blood of Pygmies peck you.

div.head: 370.—MACEDONIUS THE CONSUL
div.p: The mirror does not speak, but I will expose you who daub your counterfeit beauty with rouge. Sweet-lyred Pindar, too, once censuring this, said that “Water is best,”Ol. i. 1. water the greatest enemy of rouge.

div.head: 371.—PALLADAS
div.p: Do not invite me to witness your hunger-laden dishes, bringing me pumpkin pie to feast on. We don’t eat the solid silver you set before us, defrauding with famine fare the poor trenchers. Seek those who are keeping their fast for your display of silver, and then you will be admired for your lightly loaded plate.
